subject: business-studies
title: Porter's Five Forces Applied
welcome_lead: Use Five Forces to predict industry profit margins.
meta_desc: A-Level Strategy: applying Porter's Five Forces.
final_note: Strategy is about positioning where the forces are weakest.

concepts.def: Number, size and similarity of competitors.

walkthroughs.body_html: Industries with high rivalry, low barriers and powerful buyers (UK supermarkets) earn thin margins. Those with high barriers and weak buyers (luxury watches) earn fat margins.
Firms do not just accept forces - they reshape them. Loyalty programmes raise switching costs; patents block entry; vertical integration cuts supplier power.
Porter assumes a clear industry boundary; in digital platforms boundaries blur. Five Forces also undervalues complementors - partners whose products raise demand for yours.

options: Low margins
High margins
Zero profit
High input costs only
Porter's Five Forces are five business strategies a firm should choose between.

Competitive rivalry, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of suppliers, bargaining power of buyers — together determining industry attractiveness and potential profitability.
Porter's strategies are about marketing channels.
Porter's Five Forces are five physical security measures for a factory.

mcqs.q: What are Porter's two main generic strategies for competitive advantage?
options: Cost leadership (being the lowest-cost producer) and differentiation (offering unique value customers will pay more for) — Porter argues firms should choose one or the other.
Ansoff's Matrix shows market share against profit.
Porter's strategies are about marketing channels.
Porter says businesses should pursue both low cost and differentiation at once.

mcqs.q: What four growth strategies does Ansoff's Matrix identify?
options: Market penetration (existing product, existing market), market development (existing product, new market), product development (new product, existing market), diversification (new product, new market).
Ansoff's Matrix is about analysing competitors.
